uncited: **Inputs:** 3D object data (voxels or mesh), wavelength of light ($\lambda$), reconstruction distance ($z$).
**Outputs:** Computer-Generated Hologram (CGH) intensity/phase pattern.
*   **Layer Data:** The 3D object is divided into multiple layers according to depth cues.
Each layer contains the complex amplitude distribution of the object points at that specific depth.
*   **Hologram Plane:** A 2D grid representing the spatial light modulator (SLM) or recording medium.
**View Volume Transformation & Diffraction:** Perform Fresnel diffraction calculations for each layer using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm.
*   $U_p$ is the complex amplitude distribution on the hologram plane.
Note: The source text uses $u,v$ in the description but $p,q$ in the formula arguments; the formula explicitly maps indices $p,q$ to physical coordinates via scaling factors.
*   $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the light.
*   $k$ is the wave number, $k = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}$.
*   $U_0$ is the complex amplitude distribution of the point on the object plane.
Uses the Fresnel approximation for diffraction calculations.
Faster than angular spectrum for large distances but less accurate for very near fields. [Link to Fresnel Diffraction CGH](fresnel-diffraction-cgh.md)
Uses the angular spectrum method for exact diffraction calculations.
Suitable for both near-field and far-field holography.
More computationally intensive than Fresnel for large distances. [Link to Angular Spectrum CGH](angular-spectrum-cgh.md)
General approach of dividing 3D objects into layers and calculating holograms for each layer.
May suffer from size distortion if not using view volume transformation. [Link to Layered Rendering CGH](layered-rendering-cgh.md)
*   **Time Complexity:** Dominated by the FFT operations.
For $N$ layers and hologram size $M \times M$, complexity is $O(N \cdot M^2 \log M)$.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(N \cdot M^2)$ to store the complex amplitude distributions for all layers.
Performance depends on the number of layers and hologram resolution.
*   **When to use:** When real-size preservation of 3D objects is critical in holographic displays.

*   **When not to use:** When computational resources are extremely limited and real-time performance is not required, or when far-field holography is needed and angular spectrum might be more appropriate.
